    Higher-power Residues and Roots of Unity

    This article discusses 𝑘k-th power residues and roots of unity modulo 𝑚m, and presents algorithms for taking 𝑘k-th roots modulo 𝑚m.

    𝑘k-th Power Residues

    The study of 𝑘k-th power residues modulo 𝑚m is essentially concerned with the feasibility of taking 𝑘k-th roots modulo 𝑚m. It is a generalization of quadratic residues.

    𝑘k-th Residue

    Let 𝑘 ≥2k≥2 be an integer, and let 𝑎a and 𝑚m be coprime positive integers. If there exists an integer 𝑥x such that

    𝑥𝑘≡𝑎(mod𝑚),xk≡a(modm),

    then 𝑎a is called a 𝑘k-th residue modulo 𝑚m, and 𝑥x is a 𝑘k-th root of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m. Otherwise, 𝑎a is called a 𝑘k-th nonresidue modulo 𝑚m.

    That is, a 𝑘k-th root of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m exists if and only if 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th residue modulo 𝑚m.

    Properties

    Similar to quadratic residues, we can discuss the determination, number, and classification of 𝑘k-th residues. As with other congruence equations, we can use the Chinese Remainder Theorem to reduce them to the case of prime power moduli. Depending on the existence of primitive roots, this is further divided into odd prime power moduli and powers of 22.

    The case of odd prime powers is relatively simple. In fact, for all moduli where primitive roots exist, we have the following result:

    Theorem

    Let 𝑘 ≥2k≥2 be an integer, and let 𝑎a and 𝑚m be coprime positive integers. Suppose a primitive root modulo 𝑚m exists, and let 𝑔g be such a primitive root. Let 𝑑 =gcd(𝑘,𝜑(𝑚))d=gcd(k,φ(m)) and 𝑑′ =𝜑(𝑚)𝑑d′=φ(m)d, where 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m) is the Euler totient. Then:

    1. 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th residue modulo 𝑚m if and only if

      𝑎𝑑′≡1(mod𝑚).ad′≡1(modm).

    2. When 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th residue, there are exactly 𝑑d distinct 𝑘k-th roots of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m (up to congruence), and they have the form

      𝑥≡𝑔𝑦0+𝑖𝑑′(mod𝜑(𝑚)), 0≤𝑦0<𝑑′, 𝑖=0,1,⋯,𝑑−1.x≡gy0+id′(modφ(m)), 0≤y0<d′, i=0,1,⋯,d−1.

    3. The number of 𝑘k-th residue classes modulo 𝑚m is 𝑑′d′, and they are precisely

      {𝑔𝑑𝑖mod𝑚:0≤𝑖<𝑑′}.{gdimodm:0≤i<d′}.
    Proof

    Since 𝑎 ⟂𝑚a⟂m, we have 𝑥 ⟂𝑚x⟂m. Since 𝑔g is a primitive root modulo 𝑚m, both 𝑥x and 𝑎a are congruent to some powers of 𝑔g. Let 𝑥 ≡𝑔𝑦(mod𝑚)x≡gy(modm). The equation 𝑥𝑘 ≡𝑎(mod𝑚)xk≡a(modm) is equivalent to

    𝑔𝑘𝑦≡𝑔ind𝑔⁡𝑎(mod𝑚),gky≡gindg⁡a(modm),

    where ind𝑔⁡𝑎indg⁡a is the discrete logarithm. By the properties of order and 𝛿𝑚(𝑔) =𝜑(𝑚)δm(g)=φ(m), this is equivalent to the linear congruence

    𝑘𝑦≡ind𝑔⁡𝑎(mod𝜑(𝑚)).ky≡indg⁡a(modφ(m)).

    This is a linear congruence in 𝑦y. Applying the analysis of its solution structure from that page, we know the equation has a solution if and only if 𝑑 ∣ind𝑔⁡𝑎d∣indg⁡a, and the general solution has the form

    𝑦=𝑦0+𝑖𝑑′(mod𝜑(𝑚)), 0≤𝑦0<𝑑′, 𝑖=0,1,⋯,𝑑−1.y=y0+id′(modφ(m)), 0≤y0<d′, i=0,1,⋯,d−1.

    From this, almost all of the theorem follows. The only remaining item is the criterion 𝑎𝑑′ ≡1(mod𝑚)ad′≡1(modm). By property 3 of order,

    𝛿𝑚(𝑎)=𝛿𝑚(𝑔ind𝑔⁡𝑎)=𝜑(𝑚)gcd(𝜑(𝑚),ind𝑔⁡𝑎)=𝜑(𝑚)ind𝑔⁡𝑎.δm(a)=δm(gindg⁡a)=φ(m)gcd(φ(m),indg⁡a)=φ(m)indg⁡a.

    Since the equation has a solution if and only if 𝑑 ∣ind𝑔⁡𝑎d∣indg⁡a, i.e., 𝛿𝑚(𝑎) ∣𝑑′δm(a)∣d′, by property 2 of order, this is equivalent to the criterion.

    The case of powers of 22 is special. To handle this case, we use a result about the structure of the reduced residue system modulo 2𝑒2e: every odd 𝑎a is uniquely congruent to some integer of the form ( −1)𝑠5𝑟mod2𝑒(−1)s5rmod2e, where 𝑠 ∈{0,1}s∈{0,1} and 0 ≤𝑟 <2𝑒−20≤r<2e−2. Using this, we obtain:

    Theorem

    Let 𝑘 ≥2k≥2 be an integer, let 𝑎a be odd, and let 𝑚 =2𝑒m=2e with 𝑒 ≥2e≥2. When 𝑘k is odd:

    1. 𝑎a is always a 𝑘k-th residue modulo 𝑚m.
    2. 𝑎a has exactly one 𝑘k-th root modulo 𝑚m.
    3. The number of 𝑘k-th residue classes modulo 𝑚m is 2𝑒−12e−1, which are all the reduced residue classes.

    When 𝑘k is even, let 𝑑 =gcd(𝑘,2𝑒−2)d=gcd(k,2e−2) and 𝑑′ =2𝑒−2𝑑d′=2e−2d:

    1. 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th residue modulo 𝑚m if and only if 𝑎 ≡1(mod4)a≡1(mod4) and 𝑎𝑑′ ≡1(mod𝑚)ad′≡1(modm).

    2. When 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th residue, there are exactly 2𝑑2d distinct 𝑘k-th roots of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m, and they have the form

      𝑥≡±5𝑦0+𝑖𝑑′(mod2𝑒−1), 0≤𝑦0<𝑑′, 𝑖=0,1,⋯,𝑑−1.x≡±5y0+id′(mod2e−1), 0≤y0<d′, i=0,1,⋯,d−1.

    3. The number of 𝑘k-th residue classes modulo 𝑚m is 𝑑′d′, and they are precisely

      {5𝑑𝑖mod𝑚:0≤𝑖<𝑑′}.{5dimodm:0≤i<d′}.
    Proof

    Since 𝑎 ⟂𝑚a⟂m, we have 𝑥 ⟂𝑚x⟂m. Since both 𝑥x and 𝑎a are odd, by the above result, we can write 𝑎 ≡( −1)𝑠5𝑟(mod2𝑒)a≡(−1)s5r(mod2e) and 𝑥 ≡( −1)𝑧5𝑦(mod2𝑒)x≡(−1)z5y(mod2e). Because the representation is unique, the congruence 𝑥𝑘 ≡𝑎(mod2𝑒)xk≡a(mod2e) is equivalent to the system of linear congruences

    𝑘𝑧≡𝑠(mod2),𝑘𝑦≡𝑟(mod2𝑒−2).kz≡s(mod2),ky≡r(mod2e−2).

    Applying the analysis of linear congruences, we obtain the solution structure of 𝑥𝑘 ≡𝑎(mod2𝑒)xk≡a(mod2e). Depending on the parity of 𝑘k, there are two cases:

    • When 𝑘k is odd, since gcd(𝑘,2) =gcd(𝑘,2𝑒−2) =1gcd(k,2)=gcd(k,2e−2)=1, both linear congruences have solutions for all 𝑠,𝑟s,r. Hence the original congruence always has a solution for all odd 𝑎a.

    • When 𝑘k is even, the first equation has a solution if and only if 2 ∣𝑠2∣s, and the second has a solution if and only if 𝑑 =gcd(𝑘,2𝑒−2) ∣𝑟d=gcd(k,2e−2)∣r. Combining these gives the full set of 𝑘k-th residue classes. The first condition is equivalent to 𝑎 ≡1(mod4)a≡1(mod4); repeating the analysis for odd prime powers, the second condition is equivalent to 𝑎𝑑′ =1ad′=1. Together, these give the criterion in the theorem. The general solutions to the two linear congruences are also known:

      𝑧≡0,1(mod2),𝑦≡𝑦0+𝑖𝑑′(mod2𝑒−2), 0≤𝑦0<2𝑒−2.z≡0,1(mod2),y≡y0+id′(mod2e−2), 0≤y0<2e−2.

      Combining them gives the general solution to the original equation.

    This completely solves the determination of 𝑘k-th residues for different moduli. The Legendre symbol and quadratic reciprocity from quadratic residues can be generalized to 𝑘k-th residues, but this is not easy and requires concepts like cyclotomic fields. In algebraic number theory, quadratic reciprocity ultimately generalizes to Artin reciprocity.

    Roots of Unity

    As a special case of 𝑘k-th roots, this section discusses the concept of 𝑘k-th (primitive) roots of unity modulo 𝑚m. It can be seen as the analogue in the reduced residue system ℤ∗𝑚Zm∗ of the concept of 𝑘k-th roots of unity in the complex numbers ℂC. When the modulus 𝑚m is suitable, using 𝑘k-th primitive roots of unity modulo 𝑚m instead of the complex root 𝜔𝑘ωk can accelerate computations.

    Similar to the complex case, we have:

    𝑘k-th Root of Unity Modulo 𝑚m

    For modulus 𝑚m, a 𝑘k-th root of 11 is called a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo $m. In particular, if 𝑥x is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo $$ and is not a 𝑘′k′-th root of unity for any 𝑘′ <𝑘k′<k, then 𝑥x is called a 𝑘k-th primitive root of unity modulo $m.

    Comparing with the definition of primitive roots, a primitive root 𝑔g is a 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m)-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m, where 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m) is the Euler totient.

    When 𝑘k-th primitive roots of unity modulo 𝑚m exist, their algebraic properties match those of the primitive 𝑘k-th roots of unity 𝜔𝑘ωk in the complex numbers, and they can replace 𝜔𝑘ωk in various computations. For example, applying them to the Fast Fourier Transform yields the Number Theoretic Transform over finite fields1.

    Properties

    In the complex numbers, (primitive) roots of unity exist for any order. However, this is not the case in number theory.

    Properties

    For modulus 𝑚m, let 𝜆(𝑚)λ(m) be its Carmichael function:

    1. Every integer 𝑎a coprime with 𝑚m is a 𝛿𝑚(𝑎)δm(a)-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m, where 𝛿𝑚(𝑎)δm(a) is the order of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m.
    2. If 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m and 𝑘′k′ is any multiple of 𝑘k, then 𝑎a is also a 𝑘′k′-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m.
    3. If 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th (primitive) root of unity modulo 𝑚m, then 𝑎ℓaℓ is a 𝑘gcd(𝑘,ℓ)kgcd(k,ℓ)-th (primitive, respectively) root of unity modulo 𝑚m.
    4. As 𝑘′k′ ranges over the divisors of 𝑘k, the 𝑘′k′-th primitive roots of unity modulo 𝑚m form a partition of the 𝑘k-th roots of unity. Moreover, for ℓ ⟂𝑘ℓ⟂k, the map 𝑥 ↦𝑥ℓx↦xℓ gives a bijection between 𝑘k-th roots of unity that preserves the above partition: it maps 𝑘′k′-th primitive roots to 𝑘′k′-th primitive roots for 𝑘′ ∣𝑘k′∣k.
    5. A 𝑘k-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m exists if and only if 𝑘 ∣𝜆(𝑚)k∣λ(m). In particular, a 𝜆(𝑚)λ(m)-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m exists, called a 𝜆λ-primitive root modulo 𝑚m.
    6. An element 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m if and only if 𝑎𝑘 ≡1(mod𝑚)ak≡1(modm) and for every prime divisor 𝑝 ∣𝑘p∣k, 𝑎𝑘/𝑝 ≢1(mod𝑚)ak/p≢1(modm).
    Proof

    By the definition of order, every integer 𝑎a coprime with 𝑚m is a 𝛿𝑚(𝑎)δm(a)-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m. Conversely, if 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m, then gcd(𝑎𝑘,𝑚) =1gcd(ak,m)=1, so gcd(𝑎,𝑚) =1gcd(a,m)=1. Hence 𝑎a is a (primitive) root of unity modulo 𝑚m if and only if 𝑎a is coprime to 𝑚m. This is property 1.

    By direct verification of the definition, if 𝑘 ∣𝑘′k∣k′, then 𝑎𝑘 ≡1(mod𝑚)ak≡1(modm) implies 𝑎𝑘′ ≡1(mod𝑚)ak′≡1(modm), which is property 2. By property of order,

    𝛿(𝑎ℓ)=𝛿𝑚(𝑎)gcd(𝛿𝑚(𝑎),ℓ).δ(aℓ)=δm(a)gcd(δm(a),ℓ).

    If 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m, then 𝛿𝑚(𝑎) =𝑘δm(a)=k. Substituting gives 𝑎ℓaℓ is a 𝑘gcd(𝑘,ℓ)kgcd(k,ℓ)-th primitive root of unity. If 𝑎a is merely a 𝑘k-th root of unity, let it be a 𝑘′k′-th primitive root of unity for some 𝑘′ ∣𝑘k′∣k. Then 𝑎ℓaℓ is a 𝑘′gcd(𝑘′,ℓ)k′gcd(k′,ℓ)-th primitive root of unity. Since 𝑘′ ∣𝑘k′∣k,

    𝑘′gcd(𝑘′,ℓ)∣𝑘gcd(𝑘,ℓ),k′gcd(k′,ℓ)∣kgcd(k,ℓ),

    and by property 2, 𝑎ℓaℓ is a 𝑘gcd(𝑘,ℓ)kgcd(k,ℓ)-th root of unity. This is property 3.

    For 𝑘′ ∣𝑘k′∣k, by property 2, a 𝑘′k′-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m is necessarily a 𝑘k-th root of unity. They are pairwise disjoint, forming a partition. For ℓ ⟂𝑘ℓ⟂k, we always have ℓ ⟂𝑘′ℓ⟂k′, so for a 𝑘′k′-th primitive root of unity 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m, 𝑎ℓaℓ is also a 𝑘′k′-th primitive root of unity. Taking ℓ′ =ℓ−1mod𝑘ℓ′=ℓ−1modk, we can verify that 𝑥 ↦𝑥ℓx↦xℓ and 𝑥 ↦𝑥ℓ′x↦xℓ′ are inverse maps, so 𝑥 ↦𝑥ℓx↦xℓ is a bijection. This is property 5.

    By properties of the Carmichael function, a 𝜆(𝑚)λ(m)-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m always exists. Let it be 𝑎a, with 𝛿𝑚(𝑎) =𝜆(𝑚)δm(a)=λ(m). For 𝑘 ∣𝜆(𝑚)k∣λ(m), let 𝑘′ =𝜆(𝑚)𝑘k′=λ(m)k. Then

    𝛿𝑚(𝑎𝑘′)=𝜆(𝑚)(𝜆(𝑚),𝑘′)=𝜆(𝑚)𝑘′=𝑘.δm(ak′)=λ(m)(λ(m),k′)=λ(m)k′=k.

    Thus 𝑎𝑘′ak′ is a 𝑘k-th primitive root of unity. And by the definition of the Carmichael function, the order of all 𝑥 ⟂𝑚x⟂m divides 𝜆(𝑚)λ(m). This yields property 5.

    Property 6 follows by essentially repeating the proof of the primitive root test. This criterion actually verifies 𝛿𝑚(𝑎) =𝑘δm(a)=k.

    From these properties, we can see that relative to the case where primitive roots exist, the 𝜆λ-primitive root modulo 𝑚m plays a similar fundamental role. Unlike primitive roots, the powers of a 𝜆λ-primitive root do not generate all roots of unity modulo 𝑚m. Nevertheless, since the density of 𝜆λ-primitive roots is not low2, if one genuinely needs to find a 𝑘k-th primitive root, one can first find a 𝜆λ-primitive root by random methods, then obtain a 𝑘k-th primitive root by taking powers.

    If one 𝑘k-th root of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m is known, the set of all 𝑘k-th roots of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m can be generated from the set of all 𝑘k-th roots of unity modulo 𝑚m.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑥x be a 𝑘k-th root of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m. As 𝑟r ranges over all 𝑘k-th roots of unity modulo 𝑚m, 𝑥𝑟xr ranges over all 𝑘k-th roots of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m.

    Proof

    For two 𝑘k-th roots 𝑥,𝑦x,y of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m, let 𝑟 =𝑥−1𝑦mod𝑚r=x−1ymodm. Then 𝑟r satisfies 𝑟𝑘 ≡1(mod𝑚)rk≡1(modm), i.e., it is a 𝑘k-th root of unity. Conversely, if 𝑟r is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m, then (𝑥𝑟)𝑘 =𝑥𝑘𝑟𝑘 ≡𝑎(mod𝑚)(xr)k=xkrk≡a(modm), so 𝑥𝑟xr is a 𝑘k-th root.

    Generating all 𝑘k-th roots from 𝑘k-th roots of unity is analogous to generating the general solution of an inhomogeneous linear equation from the solution of the homogeneous one.

    The above discusses the general case. Only when primitive roots exist is the structure of roots of unity simpler:

    Theorem

    For modulus 𝑚m, suppose a primitive root modulo 𝑚m exists, and let 𝑎a be a 𝑘k-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m. Then 𝑏b is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m if and only if it can be expressed as a power of 𝑎a.

    Proof

    Let 𝑔g be a primitive root modulo 𝑚m. Then every element coprime to 𝑚m can be expressed as a power of 𝑔g. So 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m if and only if

    𝛿𝑚(𝑎)=𝛿𝑚(𝑔ind𝑔⁡𝑎)=𝜑(𝑚)gcd(𝜑(𝑚),ind𝑔⁡𝑎)=𝑘.δm(a)=δm(gindg⁡a)=φ(m)gcd(φ(m),indg⁡a)=k.

    Similarly, 𝑏b is a 𝑘k-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m if and only if

    𝛿𝑚(𝑏)=𝛿𝑚(𝑔ind𝑔⁡𝑏)=𝜑(𝑚)gcd(𝜑(𝑚),ind𝑔⁡𝑏)=𝑘′∣𝑘.δm(b)=δm(gindg⁡b)=φ(m)gcd(φ(m),indg⁡b)=k′∣k.

    Hence,

    gcd(𝜑(𝑚),ind𝑔⁡𝑎)∣gcd(𝜑(𝑚),ind𝑔⁡𝑏)∣ind𝑔⁡𝑏.gcd(φ(m),indg⁡a)∣gcd(φ(m),indg⁡b)∣indg⁡b.

    By the analysis of linear congruences, this condition is equivalent to the equation

    (ind𝑔⁡𝑎)𝑥≡ind𝑔⁡𝑏(mod𝜑(𝑚))(indg⁡a)x≡indg⁡b(modφ(m))

    having a solution. Exponentiating this condition with base 𝑔g gives 𝑎𝑥 ≡𝑏(mod𝑚)ax≡b(modm), i.e., 𝑏b can be expressed as a power of 𝑎a.

    This theorem shows that when primitive roots exist, all 𝑘k-th roots of unity form a cyclic group, and the 𝑘k-th primitive roots of unity are generators of this cyclic group. Later, we will see that the Tonelli-Shanks algorithm uses this to accelerate the discrete logarithm computation in root extraction.

    Computing 𝑘k-th Roots Modulo 𝑚m

    Finally, we discuss methods for finding 𝑘k-th roots. For 𝑘 =2k=2, there are many efficient algorithms for computing square roots modulo 𝑚m. However, for general 𝑘k, no polynomial-time algorithm is known. This section introduces two common algorithms that can find a 𝑘k-th root in 𝑂(𝑚1/2)O(m1/2) and 𝑂(𝑚1/4+𝜀)O(m1/4+ε) time respectively. Since the Chinese Remainder Theorem can always reduce the problem to prime power moduli, this section focuses on solving the prime power case.

    Naive Algorithm

    The analysis of 𝑘k-th residue properties above already points to a method for finding 𝑘k-th roots modulo prime powers. Strictly speaking, the above solved the case where the radicand 𝑎a is coprime to the modulus 𝑚m. The algorithm process is summarized as follows:

    • When 𝑚 =𝑝𝑒m=pe is an odd prime power, let 𝑔g be a primitive root modulo 𝑚m. Then the equation 𝑥𝑘 ≡𝑎(mod𝑚)xk≡a(modm) can be transformed into the linear congruence

      𝑘𝑦≡ind𝑔⁡𝑎(mod𝜑(𝑚)).ky≡indg⁡a(modφ(m)).

      Here, ind𝑔⁡𝑎indg⁡a can be found using the BSGS algorithm, and the solutions to the linear congruence are easy to find. From this, we obtain all 𝑘k-th roots 𝑥 ≡𝑔𝑦(mod𝑚)x≡gy(modm) of 𝑎a.

      There is another similar approach. Also let 𝑥 ≡𝑔𝑦(mod𝑚)x≡gy(modm), but by rewriting

      𝑥𝑘≡(𝑔𝑘)𝑦≡𝑎(mod𝑚),xk≡(gk)y≡a(modm),

      we transform it into finding the discrete logarithm of 𝑎a with base 𝑔𝑘gk. This can also be solved by the BSGS algorithm to find a particular solution. Its general solution can be obtained from the expression in the previous section, i.e., by multiplying the particular solution by all 𝑘k-th roots of unity.

      Regardless of which approach is used, when the primitive root is known, the complexity of finding a single solution is 𝑂(𝑚1/2)O(m1/2). Since a primitive root can be found in 𝑜(𝑚1/2)o(m1/2) time, the overall time complexity remains 𝑂(𝑚1/2)O(m1/2).

    • When 𝑚 =2𝑒m=2e with 𝑒 ∈ℕ+e∈N+, we can first find 𝑠,𝑟s,r in 𝑎 ≡( −1)𝑠5𝑟(mod𝑚)a≡(−1)s5r(modm). Among these two exponents, 𝑠s can be determined in 𝑂(1)O(1) time:

      𝑠={0,𝑎≡1(mod4),1,𝑎≡3(mod4).s={0,a≡1(mod4),1,a≡3(mod4).

      And 𝑟 =ind5⁡(( −1)𝑠𝑎)r=ind5⁡((−1)sa) can be found using the BSGS algorithm in 𝑂(𝑚1/2)O(m1/2) time. Next, we just need to solve the system of linear congruences:

      𝑘𝑧≡𝑠(mod2),𝑘𝑦≡𝑟(mod2𝑒−2).kz≡s(mod2),ky≡r(mod2e−2).

      The general solution (𝑧,𝑦)(z,y) is easy to find, and 𝑥 =( −1)𝑧5𝑦x=(−1)z5y is the desired root. The complexity of finding a single solution is still 𝑂(𝑚1/2)O(m1/2).

    Of course, for the case of no solution, we can quickly determine this in 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m) time using the criteria described above, without needing to determine it during the solving process.

    // Submission (TLE): https://judge.yosupo.jp/submission/320582
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <tuple>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

struct PrimePower {
  int p, e, pe;

  PrimePower(int p, int e, int pe) : p(p), e(e), pe(pe) {}
};

// Factorization.
auto factorize(int n) {
  std::vector<PrimePower> ans;
  for (int x = 2; x * x <= n; ++x) {
    int e = 0, pe = 1;
    for (; n % x == 0; n /= x, ++e, pe *= x);
    if (e) ans.emplace_back(x, e, pe);
  }
  if (n > 1) ans.emplace_back(n, 1, n);
  return ans;
}

// Binary exponentiation.
int pow(int a, int b, int m = 0) {
  int res = 1;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = m ? (long long)res * a % m : res * a;
    a = m ? (long long)a * a % m : a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

// Find a primitive root modulo prime.
int primitive_root(int p) {
  std::vector<int> exp;
  for (auto factor : factorize(p - 1)) {
    exp.push_back((p - 1) / factor.p);
  }
  int ans = 0;
  bool succ = false;
  while (!succ) {
    ++ans;
    succ = true;
    for (int b : exp) {
      if (pow(ans, b, p) == 1) {
        succ = false;
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  return ans;
}

// Discrete logarithm. (BSGS Algorithm)
int log(int g, int a, int m) {
  int b = std::sqrt(m + 0.25l) + 1;
  std::unordered_map<int, int> mp;
  int po0 = a % m, po1 = 1;
  for (int i = 0; i < b; ++i) {
    mp[po0] = i;
    po0 = (long long)po0 * g % m;
  }
  po0 = pow(g, b, m);
  for (int j = 1; j <= b; ++j) {
    po1 = (long long)po1 * po0 % m;
    if (mp.count(po1)) return j * b - mp[po1];
  }
  return -1;
}

// Extended Euclidean Algorithm.
int ex_gcd(int a, int b, int& x, int& y) {
  if (!b) {
    x = 1;
    y = 0;
    return a;
  } else {
    int d = ex_gcd(b, a % b, y, x);
    y -= a / b * x;
    return d;
  }
}

// Solves the linear congruence equation: Ax = B mod N.
// Return the least nonnegative solution and the common difference.
std::pair<int, int> solve_linear(int a, int b, int n) {
  int x, y;
  int d = ex_gcd(a, n, x, y);
  if (b % d) return {-1, -1};
  n /= d;
  x = ((long long)x * (b / d) % n + n) % n;
  return {x, n};
}

// Subroutine: Find a K-th root with a primitive root G known.
int calc(int g, int k, int a, int p) {
  int ind = log(g, a, p);
  if (ind == -1) return -1;
  int y0, d;
  std::tie(y0, d) = solve_linear(k, ind, p - 1);
  if (y0 == -1) return -1;
  return pow(g, y0, p);
}

// Find a K-th root of A modulo prime P.
int kth_roots_mod_p(int k, int a, int p) {
  a %= p;
  if (k == 0) return a == 1 ? 0 : -1;
  if (a == 0) return 0;
  return calc(primitive_root(p), k, a, p);
}

void solve() {
  int k, y, p;
  std::cin >> k >> y >> p;
  std::cout << kth_roots_mod_p(k, y, p) << '\n';
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    solve();
  }
}

    Improved Tonelli-Shanks Algorithm

    By appropriately generalizing the Tonelli-Shanks algorithm for computing square roots modulo 𝑚m, we can solve the root extraction problem for prime power moduli. A direct generalization is the Adleman-Manders-Miller algorithm3, but its complexity is still not excellent4. This section introduces the improved Tonelli-Shanks algorithm proposed by sugarknri, Min_25, 37zigen, etc. It can find a 𝑘k-th root in 𝑂(𝑚1/4+𝜀)O(m1/4+ε) time.

    The core idea of Tonelli-Shanks is to place the discrete logarithm computation in a group of order 2𝑒2e, thereby reducing the time complexity. Similarly, discrete logarithms in groups of order 𝑝𝑒pe (prime power) can be solved relatively efficiently, but the complexity is Ω(√𝑝)Ω(p). The Adleman-Manders-Miller algorithm breaks the 𝑘k-th root extraction into computing discrete logarithms in several prime power order groups, but limited by the largest prime factor 𝑝max(𝑘)pmax(k) of 𝑘k, the complexity is still Ω(√𝑝max(𝑘))Ω(pmax(k)). This algorithm further improves on this process, avoiding computing discrete logarithms for large prime factors, thereby controlling the overall complexity at 𝑂(𝑚1/4+𝜀)O(m1/4+ε).

    Process

    Consider computing a 𝑘k-th root of 𝑎a modulo a prime power 𝑚m, i.e., solving:

    𝑥𝑘≡𝑎(mod𝑚).xk≡a(modm).

    In particular, for 𝑚 =2𝑒m=2e, we also need to ensure 𝑎 ≡1(mod4)a≡1(mod4), so 𝑎a can be written as a power of 𝑔 =5g=5. Similar to the previous discussion, computing 𝑘k-th roots modulo 2𝑒2e can always be reduced to this case. When handling the case of 2𝑒2e, all 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m) mentioned in this section should be replaced with 𝛿𝑚(5) =2𝑒−2δm(5)=2e−2.

    First, the problem can be reduced to the case where the root order divides 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m). Let 𝑑 =gcd(𝑘,𝜑(𝑚))d=gcd(k,φ(m)). Then, by the properties of 𝑘k-th residues, when 𝑎a is a 𝑘k-th residue modulo 𝑚m, 𝑎a is always a 𝜑(𝑚)𝑑φ(m)d-th root of unity modulo 𝑚m. By the properties of roots of unity, for any ℓ ⟂𝜑(𝑚)𝑑ℓ⟂φ(m)d, the map 𝑥 ↦𝑥ℓx↦xℓ is a bijection between 𝜑(𝑚)𝑑φ(m)d-th roots of unity. Therefore, we can take

    ℓ=(𝑘𝑑)−1mod𝜑(𝑚)𝑑.ℓ=(kd)−1modφ(m)d.

    Raising both sides of the original congruence to the ℓℓ-th power gives

    𝑥𝑑≡𝑥𝑘ℓ≡𝑎ℓ=:𝑏(mod𝑚).xd≡xkℓ≡aℓ=:b(modm).

    The left congruence uses Euler's theorem and the following congruence (𝑐 ∈ℤc∈Z):

    𝑘ℓ=𝑑(𝑘𝑑ℓ)=𝑑(𝑐𝜑(𝑚)𝑑+1)≡𝑑(mod𝜑(𝑚)).kℓ=d(kdℓ)=d(cφ(m)d+1)≡d(modφ(m)).

    For the transformed problem, consider the prime factorization of 𝑑d:

    𝑑=∏𝑝∈ℙ𝑝𝑒.d=∏p∈Ppe.

    Starting from 𝑏 =𝑎ℓb=aℓ, for each 𝑝𝑒 ≠1pe≠1, we can successively take 𝑝𝑒pe-th roots, finally obtaining a 𝑑d-th root of 𝑏b, which is a 𝑘k-th root of 𝑎a.

    Finally, the problem reduces to solving:

    𝑥𝑝𝑒≡𝑏(mod𝑚).xpe≡b(modm).

    Let 𝜑(𝑚) =𝑝𝑠𝑟φ(m)=psr with 𝑝 ⟂𝑟p⟂r. Let 𝑞 ∈ℕ+q∈N+ be a solution to 𝑞𝑟 ≡ −1(mod𝑝𝑒)qr≡−1(modpe). Then, since 𝑏b is an 𝑟𝑝𝑠−𝑒rps−e-th root of unity, 𝑏𝑞𝑟bqr is definitely a 𝑝𝑠−𝑒ps−e-th root of unity. Let 𝜁ζ be a 𝑝𝑠ps-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m. Then 𝜁𝑝𝑒ζpe is a 𝑝𝑠−𝑒ps−e-th primitive root, so there exists ℎ ∈ℕh∈N such that 𝑏𝑞𝑟 ≡𝜁ℎ𝑝𝑒(mod𝑚)bqr≡ζhpe(modm). Then, direct verification shows

    𝑥≡𝑏(𝑞𝑟+1)/𝑝𝑒𝜁−ℎ(mod𝑚)x≡b(qr+1)/peζ−h(modm)

    is a 𝑝𝑒pe-th root of 𝑏b modulo 𝑚m.

    To compute 𝑥x, we need to find a 𝑝p-th non-residue 𝜂η modulo 𝑚m. By the properties above, we can randomly choose 𝜂 ⟂𝑚η⟂m and verify that 𝜂𝜑(𝑚)/𝑝mod𝑚 ≠1ηφ(m)/pmodm≠1. The density of such numbers is

    𝜑(𝑚)𝑚(1−1𝑝)≥14.φ(m)m(1−1p)≥14.

    Therefore, on average, we need to try at most 4 random numbers. Note that 𝜂𝑟𝑝𝑠−1 ≢1(mod𝑚)ηrps−1≢1(modm) and 𝜂𝑟𝑝𝑠 ≡1(mod𝑚)ηrps≡1(modm). So if we let 𝜁 =𝜂𝑟mod𝑚ζ=ηrmodm and 𝜉 =𝜂𝑟𝑝𝑠−1mod𝑚ξ=ηrps−1modm, they are a 𝑝𝑠ps-th and 𝑝p-th primitive root of unity respectively.

    Finally, we need to compute ℎ ∈ℕh∈N. Obviously, we can take ℎ <𝑝𝑠−𝑒h<ps−e. Consider the 𝑝p-ary representation of ℎh:

    ℎ=𝑠−𝑒−1∑𝑗=0ℎ𝑗𝑝𝑗=ℎ0+ℎ1𝑝+ℎ2𝑝2+⋯.h=∑j=0s−e−1hjpj=h0+h1p+h2p2+⋯.

    Compute these digits one by one. When the first 𝑗j digits have been computed, we must have

    (𝑏𝑞𝑟𝜁−𝑝𝑒(ℎ0+ℎ1𝑝+⋯+ℎ𝑗−1𝑝𝑗−1))𝑝𝑠−𝑒−𝑗−1≡𝜁ℎ𝑗𝑝𝑠−1≡𝜉ℎ𝑗(mod𝑚).(bqrζ−pe(h0+h1p+⋯+hj−1pj−1))ps−e−j−1≡ζhjps−1≡ξhj(modm).

    Therefore, ℎ𝑗hj can be found by computing a discrete logarithm with respect to 𝜉ξ. To achieve better time complexity, we use the BSGS algorithm. We need to compute (𝑠 −𝑒)(s−e) discrete logarithms in total. If we preprocess 𝐵B powers of 𝜉ξ, the time for a single discrete logarithm is 𝑂(𝑝/𝐵)O(p/B), and the total time complexity is

    𝑂(𝐵+(𝑠−𝑒)𝑝𝐵).O(B+(s−e)pB).

    When 𝐵 =√(𝑠−𝑒)𝑝B=(s−e)p, the total time complexity is 𝑂(√(𝑠−𝑒)𝑝)O((s−e)p). After obtaining ℎh, substituting into the expression for 𝑥x gives a particular solution.

    Time Complexity

    The time complexity of this algorithm is 𝑂(𝑚1/4+𝜀)O(m1/4+ε). In this section, we always assume a single multiplication takes 𝑂(1)O(1) time, and when computing powers, we always apply Euler's theorem for reduction, so each power computation can be done in 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m) time.

    First, consider computing a single 𝑝𝑒pe-th root. Finding a 𝑝p-th non-residue only requires testing an expected 𝑂(1)O(1) numbers, with total time complexity 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m). Computing 𝑠,𝑟,𝜁,𝜂,𝑏𝑞𝑟s,r,ζ,η,bqr each takes 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m) time. When computing ℎh, each digit requires 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m) time for power computation, and there are (𝑠 −𝑒)(s−e) digits in total, so the time complexity is 𝑂((𝑠 −𝑒)log⁡𝑚)O((s−e)log⁡m). As shown earlier, the total time for preprocessing and (𝑠 −𝑒)(s−e) queries for discrete logarithms is 𝑂(√(𝑠−𝑒)𝑝)O((s−e)p). Since 𝑠 −𝑒 ∈𝑂(log⁡𝑚)s−e∈O(log⁡m), the time complexity for a single 𝑝𝑒pe-th root is 𝑂(𝑝1/2+𝜀)O(p1/2+ε). In particular, when 𝑠 =𝑒s=e, the time complexity can be further reduced to 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m).

    Now consider the total time complexity of the algorithm. Computing 𝜑(𝑚),𝑑,ℓφ(m),d,ℓ each takes 𝑂(log⁡𝑚)O(log⁡m) time. Next, we need to factor 𝑑 =∏𝑝𝑝𝑒d=∏ppe. This step can be done in 𝑂(𝑚1/4)O(m1/4) time using the Pollard Rho algorithm. Finally, the total time complexity for sequentially computing 𝑝𝑒pe-th roots is

    𝑂(∑𝑒<𝑠𝑝1/2+𝜀).O(∑e<sp1/2+ε).

    Since for any prime factor 𝑝p with 𝑒 <𝑠e<s, 𝑝p appears at least twice in 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m), we must have 𝑝 <𝑚1/2p<m1/2. Therefore, the total time complexity is 𝑂(𝑚1/4+𝜀)O(m1/4+ε).

    In fact, in this setting, we can still achieve 𝑂(𝑚1/4+𝜀)O(m1/4+ε) time complexity without using Pollard Rho for factorization. In fact, we just need to naively trial-divide 𝑑d and only enumerate prime factors up to 𝑚1/4m1/4. Let 𝑧z be the integer after removing these small prime factors. Then for any prime factor 𝑝 >𝑚1/4p>m1/4 of 𝑧z, we must have 𝜈𝑝(𝜑(𝑚)) <4νp(φ(m))<4, where 𝜈𝑝(𝑛)νp(n) denotes the exponent of 𝑝p in the prime factorization of 𝑛n. Since we only need to consider

    1≤𝑒=𝜈𝑝(𝑑)<𝑠=𝜈𝑝(𝜑(𝑚))<4,1≤e=νp(d)<s=νp(φ(m))<4,

    there can be at most one such prime factor; otherwise, their product in 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m) would exceed 𝑚m. To isolate this (possibly existing) unique large prime factor, we just need to compute

    𝑝⋆=gcd(𝑧,𝜑(𝑚)𝑧)=∏𝑝:𝜈𝑝(𝑑)<𝜈𝑝(𝜑(𝑚))𝑝min{𝜈𝑝(𝑑),𝜈𝑝(𝜑(𝑚))−𝜈𝑝(𝑑)}.p⋆=gcd(z,φ(m)z)=∏p:νp(d)<νp(φ(m))pmin{νp(d),νp(φ(m))−νp(d)}.

    Enumerating all possibilities for 𝜈𝑝(𝑑),𝜈𝑝(𝜑(𝑚))νp(d),νp(φ(m)), the exponent of 𝑝p in this product is always 1, so what we compute is the unique large prime factor 𝑝⋆p⋆ (if it exists). As for the remaining part 𝑧/𝑝⋆z/p⋆, since it can only contain prime factors with 𝑒 =𝑠e=s, no further factorization is needed.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <tuple>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

std::mt19937 rng(std::random_device{}());

// Binary exponentiation.
int pow(int a, int b, int m = 0) {
  int res = 1;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = m ? (long long)res * a % m : res * a;
    a = m ? (long long)a * a % m : a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

// Find a P-th non-residue mod M.
int non_residue(int p, int m, int phi) {
  std::uniform_int_distribution<int> dis(1, m - 1);
  while (true) {
    int c = dis(rng);
    if (pow(c, phi / p, m) != 1) return c;
  }
  return -1;
}

// Euclidean Algorithm.
int gcd(int a, int b) { return b ? gcd(b, a % b) : a; }

// Extended Euclidean Algorithm.
int ex_gcd(int a, int b, int& x, int& y) {
  if (!b) {
    x = 1;
    y = 0;
    return a;
  } else {
    int d = ex_gcd(b, a % b, y, x);
    y -= a / b * x;
    return d;
  }
}

// Returns the modular inverse of A modulo M.
// Assumes that gcd(A, M) = 1, so the inverse exists.
int inv(int a, int m) {
  int x, y;
  ex_gcd(a, m, x, y);
  return (x % m + m) % m;
}

// Subroutine: Find a P^E-th root of A mod M.
int peth_root_mod_m(int p, int e, int a, int m, int phi) {
  int s = 0, r = phi, pe = pow(p, e);
  for (; r % p == 0; r /= p, ++s);
  int q = pe - inv(r, pe);
  int ans = pow(a, ((long long)q * r + 1) / pe % phi, m);
  int eta = non_residue(p, m, phi);
  std::unordered_map<int, int> mp;
  int zeta = pow(eta, r, m);
  int xi = pow(eta, phi / p, m);
  // Precompute powers for BSGS.
  int B = std::sqrt((s - e) * p + 0.25l) + 1;
  int pB = p / B + 1;
  int po0 = pow(xi, pB, m);
  for (int j = 1, po1 = 1; j <= B; ++j) {
    po1 = (long long)po1 * po0 % m;
    mp[po1] = j;
  }
  // Compute p-adic digits of h.
  for (int j = 0; j < s - e; ++j) {
    int err = (long long)pow(ans, pe, m) * inv(a, m) % m;
    int xi_hj = pow(err, pow(p, s - e - j - 1), m);
    long long hj = 0;
    // BSGS query.
    for (int i = 1; i <= pB; ++i) {
      xi_hj = (long long)xi_hj * xi % m;
      if (mp.count(xi_hj)) {
        hj = mp[xi_hj] * pB - i;
        break;
      }
    }
    ans = (long long)ans * pow(zeta, phi - hj * pow(p, j) % phi, m) % m;
  }
  return ans;
}

// Find a K-th root of A modulo prime P.
int kth_root_mod_p(int k, int a, int p) {
  a %= p;
  if (k == 0) return a == 1 ? 0 : -1;
  if (a == 0) return 0;
  int d = gcd(k, p - 1);
  if (pow(a, (p - 1) / d, p) != 1) return -1;
  a = pow(a, inv(k / d, (p - 1) / d), p);
  for (int dp = 2; dp * dp <= d && dp * dp * dp * dp < p; ++dp) {
    if (d % dp == 0) {
      int de = 0;
      for (; d % dp == 0; d /= dp, ++de);
      a = peth_root_mod_m(dp, de, a, p, p - 1);
    }
  }
  if (d != 1) {
    int dp = gcd(d, (p - 1) / d), de = 0;
    if (dp != 1) {
      for (; d % dp == 0; d /= dp, ++de);
      a = peth_root_mod_m(dp, de, a, p, p - 1);
    }
    if (d != 1) a = peth_root_mod_m(d, 1, a, p, p - 1);
  }
  return a;
}

void solve() {
  int k, y, p;
  std::cin >> k >> y >> p;
  std::cout << kth_root_mod_p(k, y, p) << '\n';
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    solve();
  }
}

    Handling the General Case

    Consider the general case, still with modulus 𝑚 =𝑝𝑒m=pe a prime power, but gcd(𝑎,𝑚) >1gcd(a,m)>1. If 𝑎 ≡0(mod𝑚)a≡0(modm), then

    𝑥=𝑝⌈𝑒/𝑘⌉ℓ(mod𝑝𝑒), ℓ=0,1,⋯,𝑝𝑒−⌈𝑒/𝑘⌉−1x=p⌈e/k⌉ℓ(modpe), ℓ=0,1,⋯,pe−⌈e/k⌉−1

    are all solutions to the original equation. Next, consider the case 𝑎 ≢0(mod𝑚)a≢0(modm). Let 𝑎 =𝑝𝑠𝑎′a=psa′ with 𝑝 ⟂𝑎′p⟂a′. Then let 𝑥 =𝑝𝑧𝑥′x=pzx′ with 𝑝 ⟂𝑥′p⟂x′. We have

    𝑥𝑘=𝑝𝑘𝑧(𝑥′)𝑘≡𝑝𝑠𝑎′(mod𝑝𝑒).xk=pkz(x′)k≡psa′(modpe).

    Since (𝑥′)𝑘 ⟂𝑝(x′)k⟂p, this holds if and only if 𝑘𝑧 =𝑠kz=s and (𝑥′)𝑘 ≡𝑎′(mod𝑝𝑒−𝑠)(x′)k≡a′(modpe−s). The first equation has a solution 𝑧 =𝑠𝑘z=sk if and only if 𝑘 ∣𝑠k∣s; the solution of the second equation has already been solved. Note that because the modulus of the general solution to the second equation differs from that of the original equation, each solution 𝑥′x′ of the second equation corresponds to several solutions of the original equation:

    𝑥≡𝑝𝑠/𝑘(𝑥′+ℓ𝑝𝑒−𝑠)(mod𝑝𝑒), ℓ=0,1,⋯,𝑝𝑠−𝑠/𝑘−1.x≡ps/k(x′+ℓpe−s)(modpe), ℓ=0,1,⋯,ps−s/k−1.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <tuple>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

struct PrimePower {
  int p, e, pe;

  PrimePower(int p, int e, int pe) : p(p), e(e), pe(pe) {}
};

// Factorization.
auto factorize(int n) {
  std::vector<PrimePower> ans;
  for (int x = 2; x * x <= n; ++x) {
    int e = 0, pe = 1;
    for (; n % x == 0; n /= x, ++e, pe *= x);
    if (e) ans.emplace_back(x, e, pe);
  }
  if (n > 1) ans.emplace_back(n, 1, n);
  return ans;
}

// Binary exponentiation.
int pow(int a, int b, int m = 0) {
  int res = 1;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = m ? (long long)res * a % m : res * a;
    a = m ? (long long)a * a % m : a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

// Find a primitive root modulo odd prime power.
int primitive_root(PrimePower pp) {
  std::vector<int> exp;
  int phi = pp.pe / pp.p * (pp.p - 1);
  for (auto factor : factorize(pp.p - 1)) {
    exp.push_back(phi / factor.p);
  }
  if (pp.e != 1) exp.push_back(phi / pp.p);
  int ans = 0;
  bool succ = false;
  while (!succ) {
    ++ans;
    succ = true;
    for (int b : exp) {
      if (pow(ans, b, pp.pe) == 1) {
        succ = false;
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  return ans;
}

// Discrete logarithm. (BSGS Algorithm)
int log(int g, int a, int m) {
  int b = std::sqrt(m + 0.25l) + 1;
  std::unordered_map<int, int> mp;
  int po0 = a % m, po1 = 1;
  for (int i = 0; i < b; ++i) {
    mp[po0] = i;
    po0 = (long long)po0 * g % m;
  }
  po0 = pow(g, b, m);
  for (int j = 1; j <= b; ++j) {
    po1 = (long long)po1 * po0 % m;
    if (mp.count(po1)) return j * b - mp[po1];
  }
  return -1;
}

// Extended Euclidean Algorithm.
int ex_gcd(int a, int b, int& x, int& y) {
  if (!b) {
    x = 1;
    y = 0;
    return a;
  } else {
    int d = ex_gcd(b, a % b, y, x);
    y -= a / b * x;
    return d;
  }
}

// Returns the modular inverse of A modulo M.
// Assumes that gcd(A, M) = 1, so the inverse exists.
int inv(int a, int m) {
  int x, y;
  ex_gcd(a, m, x, y);
  return (x % m + m) % m;
}

// Solves the linear congruence equation: Ax = B mod N.
// Return the least nonnegative solution and the common difference.
std::pair<int, int> solve_linear(int a, int b, int n) {
  int x, y;
  int d = ex_gcd(a, n, x, y);
  if (b % d) return {-1, -1};
  n /= d;
  x = ((long long)x * (b / d) % n + n) % n;
  return {x, n};
}

// Subroutine: Find all the K-th roots with a primitive root G known.
std::vector<int> calc(int g, int k, int a, int p, int pe) {
  int ind = log(g, a, pe);
  if (ind == -1) return {};
  int mm = p == 2 ? pe / 4 : pe / p * (p - 1);
  int y0, d;
  std::tie(y0, d) = solve_linear(k, ind, mm);
  if (y0 == -1) return {};
  int ans = pow(g, y0, pe), po = pow(g, d, pe);
  std::vector<int> res(mm / d);
  for (auto& x : res) {
    x = ans;
    ans = (long long)ans * po % pe;
  }
  return res;
}

// Find all the K-th roots of A modulo prime power P^E.
std::vector<int> kth_roots_mod_pe(int k, int a, PrimePower pp) {
  int p = pp.p, e = pp.e, pe = pp.pe;
  a %= pe;
  if (a == 0) {
    int d = pow(p, (e - 1) / k + 1);
    std::vector<int> res(pe / d);
    for (int i = 0; i < pe / d; ++i) {
      res[i] = i * d;
    }
    return res;
  }
  int s = 0;
  for (; a % p == 0; a /= p, ++s);
  if (s % k) return {};
  int psk = pow(p, s / k), pss = pow(p, s - s / k), pes = pow(p, e - s);
  std::vector<int> res;
  if (p != 2) {
    int g = primitive_root(PrimePower(p, e - s, pes));
    res = calc(g, k, a, p, pes);
  } else if (pes == 2) {
    res.push_back(a);
  } else if (k & 1) {
    int z = a % 4 == 3;
    a = z ? pes - a : a;
    res = calc(5, k, a, p, pes);
    if (z) {
      for (auto& x : res) x = pes - x;
    }
  } else {
    if (a % 4 == 3) return {};
    res = calc(5, k, a, p, pes);
    int m = res.size();
    res.reserve(m * 2);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
      res.push_back(pes - res[i]);
    }
  }
  int m = res.size();
  res.reserve(m * pss);
  for (int j = 1; j < pss; ++j) {
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
      res.push_back(res.end()[-m] + pes);
    }
  }
  for (auto& x : res) x *= psk;
  return res;
}

// Find all the K-th roots of A modulo positive integer M.
std::vector<int> kth_roots_mod_m(int k, int a, int m) {
  auto factors = factorize(m);
  int m0 = 0;
  std::vector<std::vector<int>> sols;
  for (const auto& pp : factors) {
    sols.push_back(kth_roots_mod_pe(k, a, pp));
    if (sols.back().empty()) return {};
  }
  std::vector<int> ans;
  for (int i = 0; i < (int)factors.size(); ++i) {
    auto pp = factors[i];
    if (!i) {
      m0 = pp.pe;
      ans = sols[i];
    } else {
      long long m1 = pp.pe * inv(pp.pe, m0);
      long long m2 = m0 * inv(m0, pp.pe);
      m0 *= pp.pe;
      std::vector<int> _ans;
      _ans.reserve(ans.size() * sols[i].size());
      for (auto x : ans) {
        for (auto y : sols[i]) {
          _ans.push_back((m1 * x + m2 * y) % m0);
        }
      }
      ans.swap(_ans);
    }
  }
  return ans;
}

void solve() {
  int n, m, k;
  std::cin >> n >> m >> k;
  auto ans = kth_roots_mod_m(n, k, m);
  if (ans.empty()) {
    std::cout << 0 << '\n';
    return;
  }
  std::cout << ans.size() << '\n';
  std::sort(ans.begin(), ans.end());
  for (auto x : ans) std::cout << x << ' ';
  std::cout << '\n';
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    solve();
  }
}

    #include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <random>
#include <tuple>
#include <unordered_map>
#include <vector>

std::mt19937 rng(std::random_device{}());

struct PrimePower {
  int p, e, pe;

  PrimePower(int p, int e, int pe) : p(p), e(e), pe(pe) {}
};

// Factorization.
auto factorize(int n) {
  std::vector<PrimePower> ans;
  for (int x = 2; x * x <= n; ++x) {
    int e = 0, pe = 1;
    for (; n % x == 0; n /= x, ++e, pe *= x);
    if (e) ans.emplace_back(x, e, pe);
  }
  if (n > 1) ans.emplace_back(n, 1, n);
  return ans;
}

// Binary exponentiation.
int pow(int a, int b, int m = 0) {
  int res = 1;
  for (; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = m ? (long long)res * a % m : res * a;
    a = m ? (long long)a * a % m : a * a;
  }
  return res;
}

// Find a primitive root modulo odd prime power.
int primitive_root(PrimePower pp) {
  std::vector<int> exp;
  int phi = pp.pe / pp.p * (pp.p - 1);
  for (auto factor : factorize(pp.p - 1)) {
    exp.push_back(phi / factor.p);
  }
  if (pp.e != 1) exp.push_back(phi / pp.p);
  int ans = 0;
  bool succ = false;
  while (!succ) {
    ++ans;
    succ = true;
    for (int b : exp) {
      if (pow(ans, b, pp.pe) == 1) {
        succ = false;
        break;
      }
    }
  }
  return ans;
}

// Euclidean Algorithm.
int gcd(int a, int b) { return b ? gcd(b, a % b) : a; }

// Extended Euclidean Algorithm.
int ex_gcd(int a, int b, int& x, int& y) {
  if (!b) {
    x = 1;
    y = 0;
    return a;
  } else {
    int d = ex_gcd(b, a % b, y, x);
    y -= a / b * x;
    return d;
  }
}

// Returns the modular inverse of A modulo M.
// Assumes that gcd(A, M) = 1, so the inverse exists.
int inv(int a, int m) {
  int x, y;
  ex_gcd(a, m, x, y);
  return (x % m + m) % m;
}

// Find a P-th non-residue mod M.
int non_residue(int p, int m, int phi) {
  std::uniform_int_distribution<int> dis(1, m - 1);
  while (true) {
    int c = dis(rng);
    if (gcd(c, m) == 1 && pow(c, phi / p, m) != 1) return c;
  }
  return -1;
}

// Subroutine: Find a P^E-th root of A mod M.
int peth_root_mod_m(int p, int e, int a, int m, int phi) {
  if (m == 2) return 1;
  int s = 0, r = phi, pe = pow(p, e);
  for (; r % p == 0; r /= p, ++s);
  int q = pe - inv(r, pe);
  int ans = pow(a, ((long long)q * r + 1) / pe % phi, m);
  int eta = non_residue(p, m, phi);
  std::unordered_map<int, int> mp;
  int zeta = pow(eta, r, m);
  int xi = pow(eta, phi / p, m);
  // Precompute powers for BSGS.
  int B = std::sqrt((s - e) * p + 0.25l) + 1;
  int pB = pe / B + 1;
  int po0 = pow(xi, pB, m);
  for (int j = 1, po1 = 1; j <= B; ++j) {
    po1 = (long long)po1 * po0 % m;
    mp[po1] = j;
  }
  // Compute p-adic digits of h.
  for (int j = 0; j < s - e; ++j) {
    int err = (long long)pow(ans, pe, m) * inv(a, m) % m;
    int xi_hj = pow(err, pow(p, s - e - j - 1), m);
    long long hj = 0;
    // BSGS query.
    for (int i = 1; i <= pB; ++i) {
      xi_hj = (long long)xi_hj * xi % m;
      if (mp.count(xi_hj)) {
        hj = mp[xi_hj] * pB - i;
        break;
      }
    }
    ans = (long long)ans * pow(zeta, phi - hj * pow(p, j) % phi, m) % m;
  }
  return ans;
}

// Find a K-th root of A modulo prime P^E.
int kth_root_mod_pe(int k, int a, int pe, int phi) {
  a %= pe;
  if (k == 0) return a == 1 ? 0 : -1;
  if (a == 0) return 0;
  int d = gcd(k, phi);
  if (pow(a, phi / d, pe) != 1) return -1;
  a = pow(a, inv(k / d, phi / d), pe);
  for (int dp = 2; dp * dp <= d && dp * dp * dp * dp < pe; ++dp) {
    if (d % dp == 0) {
      int de = 0;
      for (; d % dp == 0; d /= dp, ++de);
      a = peth_root_mod_m(dp, de, a, pe, phi);
    }
  }
  if (d != 1) {
    int dp = gcd(d, phi / d), de = 0;
    if (dp != 1) {
      for (; d % dp == 0; d /= dp, ++de);
      a = peth_root_mod_m(dp, de, a, pe, phi);
    }
    if (d != 1) a = peth_root_mod_m(d, 1, a, pe, phi);
  }
  return a;
}

// Subroutine: Find all the K-th roots with a primitive root G known.
std::vector<int> calc(int g, int k, int a, int p, int pe) {
  int mm = p == 2 ? pe / 4 : pe / p * (p - 1);
  int ans = kth_root_mod_pe(k, a, pe, mm);
  if (ans == -1) return {};
  int d = mm / gcd(k, mm);
  int po = pow(g, d, pe);
  std::vector<int> res(mm / d);
  for (auto& x : res) {
    x = ans;
    ans = (long long)ans * po % pe;
  }
  return res;
}

// Find all the K-th roots of A modulo prime power P^E.
std::vector<int> kth_roots_mod_pe(int k, int a, PrimePower pp) {
  int p = pp.p, e = pp.e, pe = pp.pe;
  a %= pe;
  if (a == 0) {
    int d = pow(p, (e - 1) / k + 1);
    std::vector<int> res(pe / d);
    for (int i = 0; i < pe / d; ++i) {
      res[i] = i * d;
    }
    return res;
  }
  int s = 0;
  for (; a % p == 0; a /= p, ++s);
  if (s % k) return {};
  int psk = pow(p, s / k), pss = pow(p, s - s / k), pes = pow(p, e - s);
  std::vector<int> res;
  if (p != 2) {
    int g = primitive_root(PrimePower(p, e - s, pes));
    res = calc(g, k, a, p, pes);
  } else if (pes == 2) {
    res.push_back(a);
  } else if (k & 1) {
    int z = a % 4 == 3;
    a = z ? pes - a : a;
    res = calc(5, k, a, p, pes);
    if (z) {
      for (auto& x : res) x = pes - x;
    }
  } else {
    if (a % 4 == 3) return {};
    res = calc(5, k, a, p, pes);
    int m = res.size();
    res.reserve(m * 2);
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
      res.push_back(pes - res[i]);
    }
  }
  int m = res.size();
  res.reserve(m * pss);
  for (int j = 1; j < pss; ++j) {
    for (int i = 0; i < m; ++i) {
      res.push_back(res.end()[-m] + pes);
    }
  }
  for (auto& x : res) x *= psk;
  return res;
}

// Find all the K-th roots of A modulo positive integer M.
std::vector<int> kth_roots_mod_m(int k, int a, int m) {
  auto factors = factorize(m);
  int m0 = 0;
  std::vector<std::vector<int>> sols;
  for (const auto& pp : factors) {
    sols.push_back(kth_roots_mod_pe(k, a, pp));
    if (sols.back().empty()) return {};
  }
  std::vector<int> ans;
  for (int i = 0; i < (int)factors.size(); ++i) {
    auto pp = factors[i];
    if (!i) {
      m0 = pp.pe;
      ans = sols[i];
    } else {
      long long m1 = pp.pe * inv(pp.pe, m0);
      long long m2 = m0 * inv(m0, pp.pe);
      m0 *= pp.pe;
      std::vector<int> _ans;
      _ans.reserve(ans.size() * sols[i].size());
      for (auto x : ans) {
        for (auto y : sols[i]) {
          _ans.push_back((m1 * x + m2 * y) % m0);
        }
      }
      ans.swap(_ans);
    }
  }
  return ans;
}

void solve() {
  int n, m, k;
  std::cin >> n >> m >> k;
  auto ans = kth_roots_mod_m(n, k, m);
  if (ans.empty()) {
    std::cout << 0 << '\n';
    return;
  }
  std::cout << ans.size() << '\n';
  std::sort(ans.begin(), ans.end());
  for (auto x : ans) std::cout << x << ' ';
  std::cout << '\n';
}

int main() {
  int t;
  std::cin >> t;
  for (; t; --t) {
    solve();
  }
}

    1. In fact, the modulus 𝑚m need not be prime. As long as 𝑎a is a 2𝑒2e-th primitive root of unity modulo 𝑚m, it can be used for the Number Theoretic Transform modulo 𝑚m. However, since the 2𝑒2e that needs to be handled is usually large, this means every prime factor of 𝑚m is of the form 𝑐2𝑒 +1c2e+1. Thus a single prime factor is large, and 𝑚m is usually even larger, so the general modulus case is not as commonly used as the prime modulus case. ↩

    2. From the results on the number of primitive roots, the number of 𝜆λ-primitive roots is exactly 𝜑(𝜆(𝑚))φ(λ(m)), where 𝜑( ⋅)φ(⋅) and 𝜆( ⋅)λ(⋅) are the Euler function and Carmichael function respectively. Since for almost all integers 𝑚m, 𝜆(𝑚)/𝑚 =exp⁡(−(1+𝑜(1))log⁡log⁡𝑚log⁡log⁡log⁡𝑚)λ(m)/m=exp⁡(−(1+o(1))log⁡log⁡mlog⁡log⁡log⁡m), and there exists 𝐶 >0C>0 such that for integers 𝑚 >2m>2, 𝜑(𝑚)/𝑚 =𝐶/log⁡log⁡𝑚φ(m)/m=C/log⁡log⁡m, for almost all integers 𝑚m, we have 𝜑(𝜆(𝑚))/𝑚 =exp⁡(−(1+𝑜(1))log⁡log⁡𝑚log⁡log⁡log⁡𝑚)φ(λ(m))/m=exp⁡(−(1+o(1))log⁡log⁡mlog⁡log⁡log⁡m). The 𝑜(1)o(1) in the exponent absorbs the contribution from the factor 𝜑(𝜆(𝑚))/𝜆(𝑚)φ(λ(m))/λ(m). Therefore, a 𝜆λ-primitive root can be found in expected exp⁡((1+𝑜(1))log⁡log⁡𝑚log⁡log⁡log⁡𝑚)exp⁡((1+o(1))log⁡log⁡mlog⁡log⁡log⁡m) attempts. For estimates of the Euler function, see Rosser, J. Barkley, and Lowell Schoenfeld. "Approximate formulas for some functions of prime numbers." Illinois Journal of Mathematics 6, no. 1 (1962): 64-94. For estimates of the Carmichael function, see Erdos, Paul, Carl Pomerance, and Eric Schmutz. "Carmichael's lambda function." Acta Arith 58, no. 4 (1991): 363-385. ↩

    3. The original paper is Adleman, Leonard, Kenneth Manders, and Gary Miller. "On taking roots in finite fields." In 18th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (sfcs 1977), pp. 175-178. IEEE Computer Society, 1977. A more readable introduction can be found in Cao, Zhengjun, Qian Sha, and Xiao Fan. "Adleman-Manders-Miller root extraction method revisited." In International Conference on Information Security and Cryptology, pp. 77-85. Berlin, Heidelberg: Springer Berlin Heidelberg, 2011. ↩

    4. Since this algorithm requires 𝑘k to be prime, in the worst case, we need to find a 𝑝p-th root of 𝑎a modulo 𝑚m for the largest prime factor 𝑝p of 𝜑(𝑚)φ(m). This process requires computing discrete logarithms modulo 𝑝p-th primitive roots of unity. Even with the BSGS algorithm, this takes 𝑂(√𝑝)O(p) time. However, the paper Fouvry, Étienne. "Théorème de Brun-Titchmarsh; application au théorème de Fermat." Inventiones mathematicae 79, no. 2 (1985): 383-407 shows that there exists a positive density of primes 𝑚m such that the largest prime factor 𝑝p of 𝜑(𝑚) =𝑚 −1φ(m)=m−1 is Ω(𝑚2/3)Ω(m2/3). This means the complexity of this algorithm is at least Ω(𝑚1/3)Ω(m1/3), which is worse than the improved Tonelli-Shanks algorithm presented here. ↩
